content.main_review:
This paper proposed a simple yet effective weighting strategy with random weights sampled from a distribution. 
The authors proved the convergence of RLW and revealed that RLW has a higher probability to escape local minima than existing models with fixed task weights, resulting in a better generalization ability. 
The proposed method looked elegant and novel to me.

My major concerns are three fold:
1) The authors didn't conclude / prove which distribution is best for MTL or how to choose the distribution for different datasets.
The best distribution was inconsistent across different datasets.
2) The proposed approach completely neglects the relationship between tasks, and thus it may fails in some cases where some tasks are highly correlated.
3) The reported results of RLW with different distributions and baselines were comparable (very close). I'm not sure in what extent the results can be affected by the randomness of the loss weights.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposed a simple loss weighting approach and provide proofs (I didn't not check the proof in the appendices) for convergence and generalization. The theory part looks interesting. The paper could be improved as mentioned above.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ony7
content.comment:
We thank you for the detailed and constructive comments. In the following we will make a response. If you think we have not addressed your concerns, we look forward to further discussions with you.

**Q1**: It seems the best distribution was inconsistent across different datasets, thus it is recommend to conclude how to choose the distribution for different datasets.

**A1**: Actually, in this paper, we mainly focus on proposing a more reasonable but ignored baseline, RLW, on task balancing problem in multi-task learning field. Compared with the conventional baseline like EW fixed wights in the training process, RLW is randomly weighting in each iteration, thus it is a more straightforward baseline for those state-of-the-art methods with dynamically weighting strategies. We conduct extensive experiments to show that RLW with different distributions can always outperform EW on different datasets or under different architectures, which indicates RLW is more powerful baseline than EW. Surprisingly, we find that RLW can achieve comparable performance with state-of-the-art methods and even can outperform them on some cases although different distribution is best for RLW on different cases, which further shows RLW is a better baseline than EW on task balancing problem and multi-task learning field. Therefore, we aim to demonstrate RLW is a more reasonable baseline rather than a state-of-the-art method with the best performance on all cases. To find a general distribution for RLW to achieve a better performance improvement, we will study it in the future work. We will add this discussion in the revision to better show our purpose and contribution.

**Q2**: It seems RLW completely neglects the relationship between tasks, thus it may fails in some cases where some tasks are highly correlated.

**A2**: Different from some methods like PCGrad explicitly consider the tasks' relationship in their weighting strategies, RLW implicitly considers it by the sharing pattern or architecture of the MTL model. On the other hand, how to measure the correlation between tasks is still not well addressed. According to our empirical experience, it seems the Office-31 and Office-Home datasets have highly correlated tasks, and RLW performs well on both these two datasets (in Table 10). Actually, observed from our experimental results, RLW with different distributions can always outperform EW and achieve comparable performance with state-of-the-art methods in all cases.

**Q3**: It seems the performance between RLW with different distributions and baselines were comparable, thus it is not sure in what extent the results can be affected by the randomness of the loss weight.

**A3**: Referred to **A1**.

display_title: Official Review of Paper787 by Reviewer wMzV

content.summary_of_the_paper: Here, the authors present a novel method for multitasking loss weighting called Random Loss Weighting (RLW). The method is straightforward and clearly described; RLW considers the loss weights lambda as random variables. In practice, it works by sampling the loss weights from a distribution (authors evaluated six different distributions) with some normalization and then minimizing the aggregated loss weighted by the normalized random weights. The authors provided an extensive empirical evaluation including eight state-of-the-art loss weighting strategies on six computer vision datasets and the XTREME benchmark (four multilingual problems). RWL results are comparable to previous strategies, but with a lower computational burden. The authors also provided a theoretical analysis on how the extra randomness from the sampling affects the convergence and effectiveness of RLW compared with fixed loss weights optimized via SGD.
content.main_review:
- Strengths
  - The paper provides an interesting approach in the multi-task learning field; specifically a loss weighting strategy relying on a random sampling of loss weights. In particular, it shows a comprehensive and extensive evaluation of eight loss weight strategies in orthogonal data sets of computer vision and natural language processing. To the best of my knowledge, this is the most comprehensive evaluation of weight-loss strategies (yet not the first one, perhaps cite https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?arnumber=8848395 ?). Additionally, a theoretical analysis of convergence is also provided.
  - RWL results are comparable with previous weight-loss strategies, but the relative RWL training speed over EW is faster than most methods (based on results for only one dataset - NYUV2).
- Weaknesses
  - Major
    - The paper claims that the RLW strategy is as computationally efficient as EW, but results are only provided to NYUV2 and omitted for PASCAL-Context. Is it possible to extend the “delta t” analysis to other settings such as the XTREME benchmark (5.6) and RLW with different architectures (5.7)? Specifically, DWA and UW seem to be as efficient as the proposed RLW in terms of “delta t” (table 1). In table 4, UW achieved better performances. Thus, efficiency analysis should be provided in the other datasets.
    - Six different distributions are evaluated for RLW and according to the results, there is no clear winner among these strategies. Could some discussion be added about this? Any MTL application using RLW will need to test the different distributions? Is there any practical advice other than try six additional baselines?
  - Minor
    - The paper claims in the abstract that have unified eight representative task balancing methods from the perspective of loss weighting. With this, I was expecting RLW to be a method unifying or being a generalization of all eight baselines, but it's not the case. Unify is related to categorizing these eight baselines into three different groups (learning approach, the solving approach, and the calculating approach). There is also another “unified”, which is related to the comprehensive experimental setup using these eight baselines provided. Perhaps make this "unify" term clear to the reader?
    - Negative transfer is a potential side-effect of multi-task learning and also observed when using different weight-loss strategies such as UW. Could any comment be made about how RLW could alleviate this phenomenon, or if there is any RLW feature/property that could help on this?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall,  I like the empirical evaluation of the previous loss weighting strategies using a comprehensive number of datasets in different areas. I think this is valuable and needed given the importance of these strategies in multi-task learning and the lack of evaluation for that. Also, the method proposed is quite simple, yet provides comparable results . Additionally, the paper claims that method is computationally efficient. However, the results for this claim are only partially supported leading to major concerns stated in the Weaknesses section. With this, I vote for rejecting (marginally below the acceptance threshold). Hopefully, the authors can address my concerns in the rebuttal period.

content.title: Response to Reviewer wMzV
content.comment:
We thank you for the detailed and constructive comments. In the following we will make a response. If you think we have not addressed your concerns, we look forward to further discussions with you.

**Q1**: It is recommend to provide efficiency analysis for other datasets. 

**A1**: Firstly, there is no doubt that RLW strategy is as computationally efficient as EW. As mentioned in our paper, the difference between those state-of-the-art methods lies in the way of generating the weights. In RLW, the loss weights are directly sampled from a pre-defined distribution, thus it obviously does bring negligible computational cost and also does not depend on dataset and architecture. Secondly, DWA and UW are also efficient since DWA computes weights only by the value of all task losses and UW updates weights by gradient descend. While the other methods are computationally intensive and will be affected significantly by the architecture mainly because of the computation of all task gradients. Thirdly, although UW achieves the best performance on the NYUv2 dataset under the MTAN architecture (in Table 4), it does not perform well on the other datasets or architectures. For example, the performance of UW is reduced by 0.24\% than EW on the NYUv2 dataset under the hard-parameter sharing pattern (in Table 1). However, our proposed RLW strategy can not only keep efficient but also outperform EW and achieve comparable performance with state-of-the-art methods in all cases.

To better show the efficiency of RLW, we add $\Delta^{\mathrm{d}}_{\mathrm{t}}$ as the difference of training speed between each method and EW method. Besides, we will add a section in Appendix in the revision to show the influence of network depth on the efficiency of RLW and other methods (i.e., we change the ResNet-50 backbone network into ResNet-18 or ResNet-101 under the hard-parameter sharing pattern on the NYUv2 dataset).

**Q2**: It is recommend to add some discussion about how to choose the distribution for RLW.

**A2**: Actually, in this paper, we mainly focus on proposing a more reasonable but ignored baseline, RLW, on task balancing problem in multi-task learning field. Compared with the conventional baseline like EW fixed wights in the training process, RLW is randomly weighting in each iteration, thus it is a more straightforward baseline for those state-of-the-art methods with dynamically weighting strategies. We conduct extensive experiments to show that RLW with different distributions can always outperform EW on different datasets or under different architectures, which indicates RLW is more powerful baseline than EW. Surprisingly, we find that RLW can achieve comparable performance with state-of-the-art methods and even can outperform them on some cases although different distribution is best for RLW on different cases, which further shows RLW is a better baseline than EW on task balancing problem and multi-task learning field. Therefore, we aim to demonstrate RLW is a more reasonable baseline rather than a state-of-the-art method with the best performance on all cases. To find a general distribution for RLW to achieve a better performance improvement, we will study it in the future work. We will add this discussion in the revision to better show our purpose and contribution.

**Q3**: It is recommend to make the "unify" term clear.

**A3**: There are many approaches proposed to address the task balancing problem and different methods have different motivations such as finding a common decrease direction for all task gradients in MGDA and alleviating task conflicts in PCGrad. We investigate eight representative methods among them and unify them from the perspective of loss weighting, which means those methods are essentially generating weights to linearly combine all task losses as we summarize in Table 5 in the Appendix. According to the different ways of generating weights, we further categorize those methods into three types. We will clarity this in the revision.

**Q4**: It is recommend to provide a discussion about how RLW can (help to) alleviate negative transfer phenomenon. 

**A4**: The negative transfer phenomenon in multi-task learning is still not well defined and is usually considered to have a bad performance on some tasks than the single-task counterpart. According to our empirical experience, the NYUv2 dataset suffers from such phenomenon. Observed from our experimental results on this dataset (in Table 1), most of the state-of-the-art methods are reduced the performance than EW, while RLW with different distributions can always outperform EW, which indicates RLW can slightly alleviate such phenomenon. We will add this discussion in the revision.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors propose a dynamic loss weighting algorithm that chooses random loss weights per step from a chosen distribution in a multitask setting. Model with these dynamic weights is then trained until convergence. Theoretical analysis on convergence is provided and experimental results on NYUv2, PASCAL-Context, and XTREME are given. The method seems to perform relatively on par or a bit worse compared with other SOTA methods but does not require computation of gradients.
content.main_review:
On the one hand, I think this kind of experimentation is quite necessary within multitask learning. We are starting to accrue a large number of loss-balancing methods and having an even-playing-field analysis of these methods is useful. The method proposed by the author is tested in various multitask settings and for many architectures and tends to at least come close to SOTA methods in many of these settings.

However, I find the author's proposed method rather unconvincing, for the following reasons:

- The theory of convergence is almost unnecessary in my opinion, as the authors are just adding extra zero-centered stochasticity to the training process, so of course things have similar convergence properties as the unmodified vanilla method.

- Authors do not provide sufficient analysis on how to pick the distribution, which of course is a major added hyperparameter. 

- Many results seem to somewhat underperform SOTA. While it is interesting that RLW comes close to SOTA numbers in my cases, it is known that for multitask learning models gains from even SOTA methods can be mild depending on context, so it's unclear if the presented results actually imply that RLW is performing well.

- More information needs to be provided in terms of the number of trials run for each experiment and error bars. Otherwise I believe it is not correct to provide 6 different experimental rows corresponding to RLW and then pointing out the rows which happen to perform better. Statistically, the comparison between RLW and the base SOTA methods is then not an apples-to-apples comparison. What makes this more confusing is that different distributions seem to perform better for different results. 

- Related to the last remark, how does the performance of RLW compare to performance with the optimal (through grid search) loss weights? Given that the number of tasks within the benchmarks the authors chose tends to be small (~2-4 tasks), while the only large-number-of-task dataset authors explored (CelebA) is notorious for producing rather clustered results, I would think it likely that an optimal static loss weighting might outperform RLW here as well. If so, that makes a careful statistical analysis with error bar calculations even more crucial.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe that more papers like this would be welcome additions to the multitask learning literature as they give us birds-eye views of the research landscape, but the author's approach leaves me with considerable concerns both in algorithmic design and statistical analysis of the results that need to be addressed before I am convinced this method is working as authors claim.

Thus it is important to provide a convergence guarantee for RLW and analyze its convergence properties.

**Q2**: It is recommend to provide sufficient analysis on how to pick the distribution.

**A2**: Actually, in this paper, we mainly focus on proposing a more reasonable but ignored baseline, RLW, on task balancing problem in multi-task learning field. Compared with the conventional baseline like EW fixed wights in the training process, RLW is randomly weighting in each iteration, thus it is a more straightforward baseline for those state-of-the-art methods with dynamically weighting strategies. We conduct extensive experiments to show that RLW with different distributions can always outperform EW on different datasets or under different architectures, which indicates RLW is more powerful baseline than EW. Surprisingly, we find that RLW can achieve comparable performance with state-of-the-art methods and even can outperform them on some cases although different distribution is best for RLW on different cases, which further shows RLW is a better baseline than EW on task balancing problem and multi-task learning field. Therefore, we aim to demonstrate RLW is a more reasonable baseline rather than a state-of-the-art method with the best performance on all cases. To find a general distribution for RLW to achieve a better performance improvement, we will study it in the future work. We will add this discussion in the revision to better show our purpose and contribution.

**Q3**: It is unclear whether RLW is performing well since the results of RLW comes close to SOTA methods.

**A3**: Referred to **A2**.

**Q4**: It is recommend to provide the number of trials run and error bars.

**A4**: We run EW and RLW methods in Table 1 for three times and compute the mean and standard error of $\Delta_\mathrm{p}$ as $\bar\Delta_{\mathrm{p}}$ in the following table. Specifically, we use the result of EW methods in Table 1 as the baseline result, then compute the $\Delta_\mathrm{p}$ for each running result of each method including EW, and finally calculate the mean value and standard error as $\bar\Delta_{\mathrm{p}}$. We will compute the $\bar\Delta_{\mathrm{p}}$ for all methods in all cases in the revision.

| :---- | :----: | :----: | 
| EW | $+0.00$ | $-0.085\pm0.2242$ |

content.title: Re: Response
content.comment:
Thanks to the authors for providing helpful feedback and additional comments on the paper. I have read the response and the paper again closely and have decided to keep my rating the same.

I appreciate the effort to provide standard errors but this needs to be provided for metrics in general and not just dp. dp is a strange metric in general as you usually cannot just take the average relative improvement across a set of disparate metrics and attempt to interpret the results, as this clearly is not invariant under innocuous transformations (for example, L1 vs L2). Even so, the standard error values given for dp are quite large so I would be cautious in over-interpreting them. 

My main concern is still that RLW is not convincing as an alternative method for MTL. Extensive hyperparameter search still needs to be done to figure out which distribution to draw weights from, and there is no theory to support which distribution might work. Authors seem to be proposing that RLW is a positive improvement but the improvements themselves seem somewhat marginal at best and are the result of a kitchen-sink search that has authors trying a large number of different distributions. It is a bit discouraging that authors eschew grid search as computationally intensive and yet try so many different configurations of RLW. So, without deep theoretical understandings to back it up it's difficult to endorse lukewarm numbers as sufficient evidence that RLW is an important contribution.

Alternatively, authors could contextualize RLW as a negative result - as a counterpoint to loss weighting strategies out there and to show that past loss weighting research does not work in general contexts. I would honestly find this approach potentially of high interest to the community. However, this would require additional analysis of past methods to be convincing and would require hypotheses of why past methods are insufficient, as past methods in general also are theoretically supported. 

Overall, I feel rather lukewarm on this paper because it is stuck in the middle of these two approaches - the RLW method doesn't work for me as a positive contribution as the results are lukewarm and the theory is somewhat underwhelming, but the authors also did not provide much evidence on RLW as a negative contribution. I would love to see the authors filling in the gaps in either direction and I think this type of work could be important, but in its present state I can't endorse this work for acceptance quite yet.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper conducted an empirical study of existing loss weighting based multi-task learning techniques. By comparing them in both CV and NLP multi-task benchmark datasets, the authors also identified a simple random loss weighting method achieving similar performance. This paper provided both empirical and theoretical analysis of why random loss weighting can achieve similar performance efficiently.
content.main_review:
This paper did a great job conducting empirical comparison of existing loss weighting methods for multi-task learning.

It is quite surprising to see a random loss weighting baseline achieving reasonably comparable results. But the authors not only provided theoretical analysis as well as studied the effect of RLW with different sampling distributions. 

Weaknesses
Overall I like the work and findings of this paper, but I feel like there are some places that the paper can improve.
(1) Even though the paper compared 9 state-of-the-art approaches in experiments, the discussion on the results are mostly related to RLW. It would be good to include more discussions on  when and how these existing approaches work the best.
(2) I think the experimental study can be improved by including the mean and standard-error of multiple runs.
(3) Usually these MTL methods can be strongly affected by model capacity, even though the authors mentioned DMTL (table 1) is smaller than MTAN (table 4), it is still better to see how model capacity changing in the same model architecture can affect the results of RLW and other methods.
(4) How is the other HP tuned and selected?

Nit: what does DMTL stand for?
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper conducted empirical analysis on many most recent loss weighting methods for multi-task learning, and found a simple random loss weighting approach that can achieve similar results. Even though this is quite impressive, I would love to see some experimental study with more details on standard-error of different methods, and HP tuning.
